All the time that the eye took in these light appearances and the brain passed these light criticisms, there was in the heart a barbaric pity and fear which men have never been able to utter from the beginning, but which is the power behind half the poems of the world. The mood cannot even adequately be suggested, except faintly by this statement that tragedy is the highest expression of the infinite value of human life. Never had I stood so close to pain; and never so far away from pessimism. Ordinarily, I should not have spoken of these dark emotions at all, for speech about them is too difficult; but I mention them now for a specific and particular reason to the statement of which I will proceed at once. I speak these feelings because out of the furnace of them there came a curious realisation of a political or social truth. I saw with a queer and indescribable kind of clearness what a jury really is, and why we must never let it go.

The trend of our epoch up to this time has been consistently towards specialism and professionalism. We tend to have trained soldiers because they fight better, trained singers because they sing better, trained dancers because they dance better, specially instructed laughers because they laugh better, and so on and so on. The principle has been applied to law and politics by innumerable modern writers. Many Fabians have insisted that a greater part of our political work should be performed by experts. Many legalists have declared that the untrained jury should be altogether supplanted by the trained Judge.

.....

Now, if this world of ours were really what is called reasonable, I do not know that there would be any fault to find with this. But the true result of all experience and the true foundation of all religion is this. That the four or five things that it is most practically essential that a man should know, are all of them what people call paradoxes. That is to say, that though we all find them in life to be mere plain truths, yet we cannot easily state them in words without being guilty of seeming verbal contradictions. One of them, for instance, is the unimpeachable platitude that the man who finds most pleasure for himself is often the man who least hunts for it. Another is the paradox of courage; the fact that the way to avoid death is not to have too much aversion to it. Whoever is careless enough of his bones to climb some hopeful cliff above the tide may save his bones by that carelessness. Whoever will lose his life, the same shall save it; an entirely practical and prosaic statement.

message.content:
Throughout the experience of observing the interplay of light and shadows, a profound sense of primitive compassion and dread resided in my heart—emotions that humanity has struggled to articulate since time immemorial, yet they serve as the driving force behind a significant portion of global poetry. This sentiment is difficult to encapsulate, but it can be vaguely hinted at by asserting that tragedy embodies the ultimate testament to the immeasurable worth of human existence. It was as if I had never been so intimately acquainted with suffering, nor had I ever felt so distanced from despair. Typically, I might shy away from discussing such heavy sentiments, as articulating them proves to be a formidable challenge; however, I now share these feelings for a precise reason that I will address shortly. From this emotional crucible emerged an unexpected awareness of a sociopolitical reality. I gained an unusual and almost surreal clarity regarding the true nature of a jury and the imperative need to preserve it.

Our current era has shown a persistent inclination toward specialization and professional expertise. We cultivate trained soldiers for their combat proficiency, skilled vocalists for their singing abilities, and expert dancers for their artistry, among other specialized roles. This trend has permeated the spheres of law and politics, as countless contemporary thinkers have pointed out. Numerous Fabians have advocated that a significant portion of political responsibilities should be entrusted to specialists, while many legal scholars have argued for the complete replacement of untrained jurors with professional judges.

If our world were genuinely governed by reason, one might argue that there would be little objection to this approach. However, the essence of human experience and the bedrock of all religious thought reveal a different truth. The few critical lessons that are essential for a person to grasp are often paradoxical in nature. These are principles that, despite being straightforward truths in everyday life, resist clear verbal expression without inviting apparent contradictions. For instance, it is an undeniable truth that those who derive the most joy are frequently those who do not actively seek it. Similarly, consider the paradox surrounding bravery; the notion that embracing life without an excessive fear of death is the most effective way to evade it. A person who carelessly climbs a hopeful cliff above the surf may, paradoxically, safeguard themselves through that very recklessness. The principle that losing one’s life can lead to salvation is a distinctly pragmatic observation.
